newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Oil price will rise if OPEC quotas respected - Badri.
newsitem.headline: Oil price will rise if OPEC quotas respected - Badri.

text.p: OPEC President Abdullah Salem al-Badri said on Tuesday he expected world oil prices to shore up to last year's average of over $20 a barrel if member states stopped busting production quotas set by the cartel.
"Oil prices could go up to the same levels of last year if OPEC countries respected their defined (supply) quotas," he told reporters in Abu Dhabi.
Badri is touring the region to try and underline the need for keeping output discipline to help boost prices, down more than $6 to $18 a barrel this year for benchmark Brent.

He declined to quantify quota busting. But he said some non-OPEC estimates have put actual production at 1.5 million to 2.0 million barrels per day (bpd) in excess of the official ceiling of 25.033 million bpd.
"If these estimates prove to be true, then the market would have seen an eight percent increase in production and a 20 percent fall in prices over the last three months," Badri said.
"Hence, losses of OPEC members over this period could reach $11 billion".
He said he did not seek to define a new OPEC production ceiling during his current tour ahead of the group's ministerial meeting in Vienna in June.
"We are not demanding a reduction in production...But we want a committment to quotas," said Badri, also Libya's oil minister.
He said he was confident his mission would succeed.

"I am optimistic that members will respond...I feel now, more than ever, a desire for a committment to quotas. They are also showing more understanding of the market's situation and the issue of lower prices".
Badri is expected to leave the United Arab Emirates for Saudi Arabia later today. He has already been to Qatar.

He is briefing Gulf Arab oil producers on the outcome of last week's meeting in Isfahan of OPEC's quota compliance committee. Badri has said he believed that most OPEC members would favour sticking to their current production ceiling at their June meeting.
